item.title: 'Autocratic capture': Rights groups say UAE diplomat Lana Nusseibeh too dangerous to lead UN
item.description:
'Autocratic capture': Rights groups say UAE diplomat Lana Nusseibeh too dangerous to lead UN

Submitted by Yasmine El-Sabawi on Tue, 10/27/2026 - 16:10
Nusseibeh has spent the last three years denying her country's role in the genocide in Sudan
Minister of State at the Ministry of Foreign Affairs of the United Arab Emirates, Lana Nusseibeh, attends a meeting with foreign ministers of the GCC member states and the US Secretary of State, in Manama, Bahrain, on 25 June 2026 (Eric Lee/Pool via AFP)
Off

Rights groups on Tuesday called on members of the United Nations to oppose the candidacy of an Emirati diplomat who has consistently denied her country's involvement in propping up what has been termed a genocide in Sudan, deeming her too dangerous to the international order.

Last week the United Arab Emirates formally nominated Lana Nusseibeh, its former ambassador to the United Nations and current minister of state at the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, to succeed Antonio Guterres as the body's secretary general, adding a last-minute contender to a deadlocked race.

Her candidacy drew immediate criticism, owing to the UAE's support for parties accused of genocide, namely the breakaway paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF) in Sudan, as well as Israel, whose acts of genocide in Gaza continue despite a year-long ceasefire. 

Some members of the former Biden administration, as well as other former US diplomats, praised her on social media, and Abu Dhabi's close ties with Washington may indeed prove a boon for her candidacy.

Middle East Eye also learned this week that the UK is leaning towards backing her nomination.

The UN has never had a woman be its chief, and certainly not one with Palestinian roots, hailing from a well-known Jerusalemite family. 

But rights groups on Tuesday argued she is far too dangerous to take on the role. 

"We cannot afford to have the UN led by somebody who is a genocide denier, and indeed somebody who heads a government that has been aiding and abetting genocide, that is basically criminally complicit in that genocide, and she's a lead person in covering that up," Kenneth Roth, the former executive director of Human Rights Watch, said on a joint virtual panel on Tuesday that called for Nusseibeh's disqualification.

"This is the opposite of the kind of moral standing, the human rights leadership that we want from a UN secretary general," he added. 

Kate Ferguson, co-executive director of the UK non-profit Protection Approaches, called Nusseibeh's bid "autocratic capture of our most significant multilateral institution".

"None of us are safer with a captured United Nations, and while our insecurity will be unequal, all of us will become less safe if this candidacy is allowed to proceed," she said.

"There is not, as far as I have seen, sufficient evidence that this candidate is independent from the state from which she comes, and we must not be naive... that this is not a calculated effort of autocratic capture, backed by the United States, to seize and asset-strip the United Nations." 

'Blocked' every pathway to justice

This week marked the one-year anniversary of the RSF's takeover of Sudan's southwestern city of El Fasher, in the North Darfur region, where now only 70,000 people remain from what humanitarian organisations and the Sudanese government said were upwards of a million displaced people seeking safety there last year. 

"Unlawful killings, detention and torture... [and] surveillance" are "rife" in the city, Amnesty International said, based on new survivor testimonies. 

"The United States government determined that RSF committed genocide in February 2025, and put sanctions on seven of the companies [backing] the RSF, and those companies were either based on the UAE or linked directly to the United Arab Emirates," Ibrahim Alduma, who is from El-Fasher and is co-founder of Sudan Action Hub, said on Tuesday's panel.

Sudan decries Nusseibeh UN candidacy as ‘whitewashing' Emirati role in civil war
Read More »

Washington followed up that determination with an "agreement of $6.4bn of international trade between the UAE and the United States, and this is one of the main things we need to stop", he added.

According to the Center for International Policy, the UAE has received well over $2bn in US military deliveries alone since January 2025. 

"The second thing that we are talking about is the partnership between the UAE and the US and the AI, because the UAE cannot do anything with the AI without the chips of the United States," Alduma said. 

The US artificial intelligence corporation Anthropic said last month it had disrupted a UAE-directed influence operation using its own tools, and that the operation was designed to change perceptions of Abu Dhabi vis-a-vis the civil war in Sudan. 

"This lady has blocked every justice pathway that could be achieved for the people of El Fasher or Sudan, and what [the] UAE is doing with [the] RSF is a closed loop support," Alduma said. "Not only the military support and enabling them to committing the genocide, but also the international [community] covering through different ways, different means."

The UAE continues to deny its involvement in the war, despite mounting evidence reported on by Middle East Eye's correspondents, human rights organisations, and the UN itself.

UAE role in Sudan

Nathaniel Raymond, the executive director of the Humanitarian Research Lab at the Yale School of Public Health, laid out how his team tracked the way technical military support from the UAE to the RSF allowed for the takeover of El Fasher, as well as the killing of more than 150,000 Sudanese, and the displacement of 12 million others since April 2023. 

The RSF's objective, "which they clearly stated, was not only to defeat the Sudanese Armed Forces in El Fasher... but it was specifically to hunt and kill Zagawa and Fur people", referencing two of the targeted ethnic groups. 

Sudan is home to at least 500 ethnic groups. 

"The UAE made it possible technically for the RSF to... effectively trap and kill civilians," Raymond said. 

He pointed to intelligence sensor reconnaissance drones which the RSF has used to find out where civilians were hiding.

"They also did another thing. They blocked phone communications," he explained. "They prevented civilians from being able to call for help and from being able to access the internet, and in the last 72 hours... there was a full blackout that was caused by drones as people were trying to escape, so they couldn't call for help and they couldn't send images." 

Exclusive: UK leans towards backing UAE's Lana Nusseibeh for UN secretary-general
Read More »

There is also the observable and swift upgrade of armaments used by the RSF, which had previously only stolen weapons from the Sudanese army, Raymond noted. The RSF's AH4 howitzers - a lightweight artillery gun capable of continuous firing at two rounds per minute - could only have come from the UAE, he said.

"The RSF 20 years ago was the Janjaweed, and the weapons systems they had were basically horses, camels, pickup trucks, Enfield rifles, AK-47s. Suddenly, cut forward 20 years, they have an air force. They have electronic jamming capability. They have advanced mapping and tracking capability for civilians, including quadcopters, hexcopters. None of that came out of nowhere."

Last week, Amnesty International reiterated its years-long call for an "immediate ceasefire" and the "urgent deployment of an international force to protect civilians".

"All countries must also immediately stop providing arms and ammunition to all parties to the conflict in Sudan," it said. "In particular, all countries must cease arms transfers to the United Arab Emirates until it stops supplying weapons to RSF in violation of the UN embargo on Darfur. The UN Security Council must also expand the existing arms embargo on Darfur to the rest of the country."

While the Trump administration's African affairs envoy, Massad Boulos, appeared to prioritise a diplomatic solution earlier this year, there has been little to no known movement on that front since.

item.title: Israel election commission rejects Netanyahu party bid to extend voting
item.description:
Israel election commission rejects Netanyahu party bid to extend voting

Israel's Central Elections Committee on Tuesday rejected a request by Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's party to extend voting beyond 10pm local time.

"High nationwide turnout across all sectors of society reflects strong public engagement in the democratic process, and no need to extend voting hours was identified," a commission statement said.

item.title: Oman calls for Gulf, Iraq and Iran to unite under one security pact
item.description:
Oman calls for Gulf, Iraq and Iran to unite under one security pact

Submitted by MEE staff on Tue, 10/27/2026 - 16:59
Antagonism against Iran imposed by the US comes at 'a terrible cost' for the region, Oman's foreign minister says
Omani Foreign Affairs Minister Badr al-Busaidi gives a thumbs up as he leaves his hotel to reach the Omani ambassador's residence for talks between the US and Iran in Geneva, on 26 February 2026 (Fabrice Coffrini/AFP)
Off

Omani Foreign Minister Badr al-Busaidi has called on the six Gulf countries, Saudi Arabia, Bahrain, Kuwait, Qatar, the UAE, and Oman, as well as Iraq and Iran, to unite under a single "non-aggression" security pact.

Speaking at the UK's Cambridge University on Monday during a diplomatic visit, Busaidi said it was time for the Gulf "to step up and take responsibility for our own security" and end reliance on "external powers".

"The nuclear issue and the Hormuz issue are both impossible to resolve because external powers continue to define the terms of engagement, while regional powers are unable to take collective responsibility for making their own security arrangements and reach a consensus on them," Busaidi said.

"That is why in my talk today I am making a call for us in the Gulf to step up and take responsibility for our own security, and for us to do so inclusively." 

His speech came amid a flurry of diplomatic activity surrounding Iran, including senior officials from the Mecca Defence Alliance meeting Iranian leaders in Tehran on Monday.

Iran's top security official, Mohsen Rezaei, said the talks showed that US threats had little impact on regional diplomacy and marked the start of a "real transformation".

Members of the alliance - Saudi Arabia, Turkey, and Pakistan - gathered to negotiate as regional powers strive to end the Israeli-US war against Iran and establish a security framework independent of Washington.

The talks come as the conflict continues to threaten the region and the global economy, amid mounting fears of renewed US-Israeli attacks.

'False perception' of antagonism against Iran

Busaidi said that positioning Iran as the security threat has been "the most damaging of the priorities imposed on the region from the outside".

"This produced an unstable regional system constructed on the entirely false perception that there is a fundamental regional antagonism between Iran and the Arab states of the Gulf," he said.

"There is no such fundamental antagonism."

While problems exist, Arabs and Persians have lived in peace in the Gulf for centuries, he added.  

Iran will not trade its nuclear insurance policy for worthless American promises
Read More »

"Any Gulf security architecture that doesn't include [Iran] is inherently unstable. It's structurally unsound," he said.

"And recent events expose the terrible cost of allowing the false perception of antagonism and exclusion."

Since the US and Israel launched their war on Iran on 28 February, Gulf Arab countries have voiced frustration over the US failing to provide security against retaliatory attacks from Iran, which had targeted US military bases in the region.

The US-Israel war on Iran has inflicted massive economic and security costs on Gulf countries. 

By late March, the war had battered the UAE's economy, wiping more than $120bn from market capitalisation on the Dubai and Abu Dhabi stock exchanges, while over 18,400 flights were cancelled.

The economic repercussions of the ongoing blockade of the Strait of Hormuz have also reverberated worldwide.

Busaidi said the region can no longer rely on cooperation from external partners and that the goal should be a "non-aggression pact" among the Gulf states.

"The time has come when it no longer makes sense just to blame everyone else," he said.

"We need to begin a new regional dialogue on Gulf security, and we need to do so before other solutions are imposed on the region, which would effectively consolidate the pattern of dependency and exclusion for which we urgently need to find an alternative."

He added that over time, external partnerships, such as with the US, would involve less military commitments and more economic and investment partnerships.

item.title: Smotrich says ‘Arab turnout unprecedented’
item.description:
Smotrich says ‘Arab turnout unprecedented’

Israel’s far-right Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich has urged right-wing voters to cast their ballots, claiming that unprecedented turnout among Palestinian citizens of Israel could help bring a “dangerous left-wing government” to power.

“Do not despair! It is still possible to win,” Smotrich said in a post on X.

Palestinian politicians have accused right-wing figures of incitement against Palestinian citizens of Israel, who make up 20 percent of the country’s population.

Ra’am says Israeli police seized ballot boxes in Negev

Israeli police have seized ballot boxes in the town of Arara in the Negev, Al Jazeera reported, citing Mansour Abbas’s Ra’am, also known as the United Arab List.

item.description:
Ra’am’s Abbas calls for sustained voting to ‘bring down’ Netanyahu

Netanyahu is using the political group as a “scarecrow” to mobilise right-wing voters, Mansour Abbas, the leader of Ra’am, or the United Arab List, said.

Abbas wrote in a social media post that the United Arab List appeals to our people for their support and votes” and added that his party “will bring down Benjamin Netanyahu, Smotrich, and Ben Gvir in this election”.

item.title: Netanyahu warns of Arab voter surge in Israel's election in desperate bid to woo support
item.description:
Netanyahu warns of Arab voter surge in Israel's election in desperate bid to woo support

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and his far-right coalition partners made a last-ditch push on Tuesday to get their supporters to the polls, warning of a surging Arab voter turnout, a tactic Palestinian politicians denounced as racist and inflammatory.

Cars flying Netanyahu's Likud party flags drove through Jerusalem blaring the Islamic call to prayer and urging supporters to cast their ballots because "Arabs are voting", witnesses said.

"If we don't wake up now, we'll find ourselves with a government of Mansour Abbas and Ahmed Tibi," Netanyahu wrote in a post, referring to two leading Palestinian politicians in Israel.

Tibi, a candidate from an Arab party, said strong turnout among Israel's Arab minority would "pave the way for an alternative government and change the grave reality".

Sami Abu Shehadeh, leader of the Arab Balad party, wrote on X that long lines outside polling stations should bring "pride and joy to anyone who believed in democracy".

"We are receiving all these inciting messages from the petty racists, Ben Gvir, Netanyahu, and their partners. What are they afraid of? This is actually an excellent sight, it is good for democracy."

item.title: Party of main Netanyahu challenger opposes bid to extend Israel voting hours
item.description:
Party of main Netanyahu challenger opposes bid to extend Israel voting hours

The party of Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's main election challenger said it "firmly opposes" a call from the premier's party to extend voting hours on Tuesday, calling it a pretext for a future challenge to the poll's legitimacy.

"No exceptional incident has occurred that would justify granting this request, which is intended to lay the groundwork for allegations challenging the integrity of the election, continuing the lies Netanyahu has been spreading since this morning," ex-army chief Gadi Eisenkot's Yashar party said.

item.title: Who is Lana Nusseibeh, the UAE diplomat in the race to become next UN secretary-general?
item.description:
Who is Lana Nusseibeh, the UAE diplomat in the race to become next UN secretary-general?

Submitted by Daniel Tester on Tue, 10/27/2026 - 14:52
Critics have objected to how she has represented the UAE on Sudan, Israel-Gaza, Libya, Yemen and Somaliland among others
UAE Minister of State at the Ministry of Foreign Affairs Lana Nusseibeh at the UN HQ in New York on 7 April 2026 (Reuters)
On

The Emirati diplomat and minister Lana Nusseibeh has emerged as a late contender in the contest for the next UN secretary-general.

The UAE announced her last-minute candidacy earlier this month, amid a stalemate to choose a successor to Portuguese incumbent Antonio Guterres, whose 10-year term ends on 31 December.

The successful candidate is usually selected by the 15-member UN Security Council (UNSC), before the recommendation is rubber-stamped by the wider UN General Assembly (UNGA). Traditionally the role rotates between continents: many believe that a female diplomat from Latin America should occupy the position.

No clear consensus has emerged from the UNSC after six anonymous straw polls, with all candidates so far facing opposition from the veto-wielding permanent members, namely the US, UK, France, Russia and China.

While political power in the UN is primarily held by the UNSC and the UNGA, the secretary-general has an important administrative and agenda-setting role and is the public face of the organisation.

But the candidacy of Nusseibeh, a top minister in the UAE’s foreign office and a former Emirati ambassador to the UN, has been criticised.

As the Emirate’s UN representative, she has consistently denied it is involved in Sudan’s ongoing civil war, despite considerable evidence of the UAE backing the Rapid Support Forces (RSF), a paramilitary group accused of war crimes and other atrocities.

Questions have also been raised about the UAE’s relationship with Israel, which has killed at least 74,000 Palestinians in Gaza since October 2023 in what leading human rights organisations and a UN commission have referred to as  genocide.

Here’s what you need to know about Nusseibeh, her involvement in major Middle East issues and what her leadership of the UN could mean.  

Nusseibeh’s early life

Lana Nusseibeh, who was born in 1978 in Abu Dhabi, is a member of a prominent, aristocratic family from Jerusalem that has been politically active for decades. 

Her grandfather, Anwar Nusseibeh, who lost a leg during the Nakba, held ministerial roles in Jordan in the 1950s when it controlled the West Bank and East Jerusalem. Sari Nusseibeh, her uncle, is a prominent Palestinian intellectual who was an aide to Yasser Arafat during the early 2000s.

In 1967, her father, Zaki Nusseibeh, settled in Abu Dhabi amid the 1967 Middle East War. Then in his twenties, he was an interpreter for Sheikh Zayed, the UAE’s founding father. He has remained in Abu Dhabi’s upper echelons since, serving as a foreign affairs minister from 2017 to 2021. 

Lana Nusseibeh attended first the British School al Khubairat in Abu Dhabi and later Wycombe Abbey, a private girl’s school in High Wycombe, north-west of London.

She then studied history at Queen’s College, Cambridge and a master’s in Israeli and Jewish Diaspora Studies at the School of Oriental and African Studies, University of London, graduating in 2003. She speaks English, French and Hebrew besides Arabic.

What’s been Nusseibeh’s career path?

Nusseibeh joined the UAE’s ministry of foreign affairs in 2006, after consulting for Unesco and the Gulf Research Centre think tank. 

She led its policy planning department from 2010 to September 2013, when the UAE cracked down on dissent amid the Arab Spring and was accused of supporting the military overthrow of Egyptian president Mohamed Morsi in July 2013. She was the UAE’s permanent representative to the UN from 2013 until April 2024.

Nusseibeh’s official platform as to what she would do if she became secretary general is vague - not unusual, given the complex diplomacy that candidates must navigate to successfully secure the top job. She says that her priorities as secretary-general would be to “act earlier, bridge divides and pursue practical first agreements”, and to “protect essential aid while helping countries mobilise investment, address debt and shape their own development”.

She also discusses defending the UN charter, international law and universal human rights, “consistently and without double standards”.

Critics of Nusseibeh’s candidacy have pointed to the UAE’s human rights record, including accusations of unfair detention, torture, and widespread exploitation of migrant workers.

What has Nusseibeh said about Sudan?

Nusseibeh’s UN tenure overlapped with a period when the UAE developed a far more assertive foreign policy, supporting warring parties in civil conflicts from Libya to  Yemen.

The UAE’s role in Sudan, which is subject to a UN arms embargo, has attracted especial attention, with rights organisations and UN investigators criticising its backing for the RSF, which the UN says has committed atrocities that bear the “hallmarks of genocide”.   

In April 2024, Nusseibeh told the UN Security Council that such allegations were “spurious, unfounded, and lack[ing] any credible evidence”.

Her letter described Sudanese concerns about Emirati involvement in the conflict as “nothing more than an attempt to divert attention”, and added that the UAE was “profoundly concerned about the dissemination of disinformation and false narratives”. 

Nusseibeh has continued to defend UAE policy in Sudan since she left her ambassadorial job the same month to become the UAE’s Assistant Minister for Political Affairs and Envoy of the Minister of Foreign Affairs.

Asked by CNN in July 2024 if she rejected UN investigators’ findings of “credible” evidence of Emirati support for the RSF, Nusseibeh said: “Absolutely”, adding that such allegations were “categorically untrue”.

And in November 2025, Nusseibeh travelled to Strasbourg to lobby the European Parliament to remove references to the UAE’s role in Sudan from an EU resolution condemning atrocities. The UAE was not mentioned in the final resolution.

In a statement to Middle East Eye, Sudan’s UN mission accused Nusseibeh of “defending and whitewashing her country’s record of troubling the peace of Sudan by enabling genocide, enslaving our women and girls and instigating sexual violence and other atrocities, in addition to destabilising our sovereignty.

“The UAE must face accountability, not to be rewarded with the top global leadership role of the UN.”

As secretary general, Nusseibeh would be bound by the UN Charter to act independently of all governments, including Abu Dhabi. 

But Ammar Mahmoud, a top Sudanese diplomat at the UN, said her outright rejection of the UN investigators' findings on Emirati involvement signalled she would not undertake the role with due impartiality. 

"I highly doubt that she will ever form any investigative committees about the UAE’s role in Sudan,” Ammar Mahmoud, a top Sudanese diplomat at the UN, told Middle East Eye.

“Nor do I think that she will accurately reflect, in her engagements with world leaders as secretary-general, the true nature of the conflict in Sudan and her country’s role in it.”

What has Nusseibeh said about Israel and Gaza?

Mediating the Israel-Palestine conflict would be an immediate demand on the next secretary general. But Nusseibeh faces questions about her willingness to hold Israeli leaders to account for alleged war crimes committed in Gaza.

Although the UAE has repeatedly voted against Israel at the UNGA, Abu Dhabi and Israel have had strong relations since they signed the US-brokered Abraham Accords in 2020, a landmark deal championed by Nusseibeh that ended decades of diplomatic boycott.

Last week, Israeli prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu gave a security presentation outlining an “Israel-UAE Hexagon Alliance”, which also appeared to name Sudan’s RSF as a “friendly” party. 

Abu Dhabi’s official position is to call for self-determination for Palestinians via the two-state solution, although this has long been rejected by Israel. Nusseibeh said in September 2025 that Israel’s formal annexation of the West Bank would be a “red line” for the UAE. She has also promoted the UAE’s role in providing aid to the besieged Gaza Strip.

But diplomats who have worked with Nusseibeh suggest that the Emirate’s stance on Israel is closer than official statements might suggest. “The UAE is totally aligned with Israel”, a European official who sat in on a diplomatic meeting between Nusseibeh and her US counterparts in the summer of 2026 told Middle East Eye, adding that there appeared to be “no limits” to the states’ relationship. 

What else has Nusseibeh and the UAE said about the Middle East?

Libya: The UAE has been implicated in war crimes in Libya, where it is accused of backing Khalifa Haftar, whose Libyan Arab Armed Forces controls swathes of the country’s east.

In 2015, leaked internal Emirati emails revealed that the UAE was secretly shipping weapons to its allies in Libya despite a UN arms embargo. The emails included messages sent directly to Nusseibeh, which critics said showed that she had explicit knowledge of the arms transfers.

UN investigators later found that the UAE, along with Turkey and Jordan, had systematically violated the arms embargo. Nusseibeh refused to comment.

Gulf states: Nusseibeh was at the centre of a diplomatic crisis when, in June 2017, the UAE, along with Saudi Arabia, Bahrain and Egypt, cut ties with Qatar over Doha’s alleged support for “terrorism”. 

The crisis escalated to an effective blockade of Qatar’s land and sea borders. At the UN, Nusseibeh rallied support for the blockade, describing the measures in 2017 as “entirely legal, justified and proportionate”. Relations between Qatar and the UAE have since impoved. 

Yemen: The UAE backs the Southern Transitional Council (STC), a secessionist movement that wants independence for parts of southern Yemen amid Houthi control of the north.  

This support caused another diplomatic crisis earlier this year, when the STC’s failed push to expand its territorial control prompted a major fallout between Abu Dhabi and Saudi Arabia, which opposes the break-up of Yemen.  Saudi Arabia, along with the rest of the GCC, has nonetheless backed Nusseibeh’s candidacy. 

Somaliland: Nusseibeh’s campaign has been endorsed by the breakaway territory from Somalia that is recognised only by Israel. The UAE has fostered strong, informal ties with Somaliland, where it has built military bases and port infrastructure.

The territory wants to join the UN: the secretary-general can push for the admission of new members, although final authority rests with the Security Council and the UNGA. Nusseibeh is yet to give her stance.

Western Sahara: At the UNGA in 2025, Nusseibeh offered the UAE’s “full support for Moroccan sovereignty over the Moroccan Sahara”. 

Morocco claims sovereignty over the region, which is recognised by the UN as a non-self-governing territory given the competing claims of the indigenous Sahrawi people, led by the Polisario Front. 

Nusseibeh has said that the UAE endorses “the Autonomy Initiative within the framework of Moroccan territorial integrity”, which would grant Western Sahara limited self-government under Moroccan control. The plan is backed by the UK, US and France, but opposed by neighbouring Algeria, which cut ties with the UAE in September. 

Diplomacy
Who is Lana Nusseibeh, the UAE diplomat hoping to become the next UN secretary-general?

item.title: UN inquiry finds Israel committed age-based persecution of Palestinian children in West Bank
item.description:
UN inquiry finds Israel committed age-based persecution of Palestinian children in West Bank

Israeli authorities and forces have committed the crime against humanity of age-based persecution against Palestinian children in the occupied West Bank, the UN's top investigative body on Palestine and Israel has concluded, while also accusing Israel of continuing its genocide in Gaza despite a ceasefire agreement.

In its fifth report to the UN General Assembly, published on Monday, the Independent International Commission of Inquiry on the Occupied Palestinian Territory, including East Jerusalem, said Israeli forces had "deliberately killed and caused serious bodily and mental harm to Palestinian children on account of their status as Palestinian children".

The report said the harm inflicted on children "is not incidental or collateral" to the wider violence, but "forms part of a pattern of intentional violence directed against Palestinian children", amounting to the crime against humanity of persecution. 

Read more: UN inquiry finds Israel committed age-based persecution of Palestinian children in West Bank

item.title: Israeli voter: 'A vote against fear, terror and inequality'
item.description:
Israeli voter: 'A vote against fear, terror and inequality'

An Israeli voter has told Middle East Eye that current elections in Israel were existential.

Fatima Hassan Bakri, a 77-year-old Palestinian citizen of Israel, said this was the first time she had "felt the weight of the moment as I cast my ballot, because these elections are different from any other."

"This vote is a vote for survival and for our very existence. A vote for our children who emigrate because there are no jobs. A vote against fear, terror and inequality," she said.

"I call on every woman to come out and vote with her children. We make up half of society, so we should make our voices heard."

item.title: Israeli voter: 'This government is racist'
item.description:
Israeli voter: 'This government is racist'

Getting rid of Netanyahu's "racist" government should be a priority for Israelis, an Israeli voter told Middle East Eye.

Kassim Titi, a Palestinian citizen of Israel from the Galilee, said that the Israeli prime minister and his far-right allies Itamar Ben-Gvir and Bezalel Smotrich had fomented severe hatred against Palestinians.

He said the "government is racist and led by Ben Gvir and Smotrich."

"The way they treat Arabs is not right. We want to live in peace, stability and security and we want equality between Jews and Arabs," he said.

item.title: Egypt jails Mada Masr editor and orders outlet closed
item.description:
Egypt jails Mada Masr editor and orders outlet closed

Submitted by MEE staff on Tue, 10/27/2026 - 13:41
The conviction of respected journalist Lina Attalah and the closure of the independent news site represents a devastating blow to press freedom in the country
Egyptian journalist Lina Attalah, co-founder and editor-in-chief of the Cairo-based online newspaper Mada Masr, pictured during an interview with AFP in Cairo, Egypt, 28 December 2020 (AFP)
Off

Security personnel lifted prominent Egyptian journalist Lina Attalah off the ground and carried her out of a Cairo courtroom on Tuesday, moments after a judge convicted the Mada Masr editor-in-chief of running an unlicensed website and ordered the independent outlet closed.  

Attalah remained in custody at the courthouse on Tuesday afternoon, the outlet said.  

The ruling is the harshest outcome yet in six years of legal cases against Mada Masr, one of the few independent outlets still operating in Egypt under the authoritarian government of President Abdel Fattah el-Sisi.   

The ninth circuit of the New Cairo Misdemeanour Court, presided over by Judge Mohamed Mubarak, imposed the maximum penalty: a fine of 3m Egyptian pounds (around $53,500), the closure of Mada Masr's website and the confiscation of its property.  

Hossam Bahgat, executive director of the rights group Egyptian Initiative for Personal Rights, who attended the hearing, told Mada Masr that after deliberations the judge cleared the courtroom of everyone except Attalah and her lawyers.   

Plainclothes officers and guards then filled the room, with a National Security Agency officer present, he said.  

The judge, joined by a representative of the Supreme State Security Prosecution, upheld his rejection of all procedural requests from the defence, including to submit documents and hear witnesses. The defence refused to enter a plea while those requests went unanswered.    

The judge then called for a lawyer unknown to the defence team and appointed him to represent Attalah, "in a move that astonished all those present", Bahgat said.    

'If Egypt can put in custody one of its most respected editors and shut down her newsroom, no independent journalist in the country is safe'

- Sara Qudah, CPJ regional director

Her eight lawyers objected, and Attalah told the court she did not accept the appointment. The judge refused to record her objection in the minutes. 

"In an even more shocking move," Bahgat said, the judge himself began writing down requests attributed to the court-appointed lawyer, who had not spoken. The verdict was then read out over shouts from the defence. 

Media freedom rights group Committee to Protect Journalists (CPJ) denounced Attalah's detention as an attack on free speech.   

“The conviction of Lina Attallah and the order to shut down Mada Masr represent a devastating blow to press freedom in Egypt and a direct message aimed at dismantling independent media in the country,” said CPJ Regional Director Sara Qudah.   

“Attalah and Mada Masr are among the most prominent voices in Egypt’s independent media landscape, providing critical reporting on issues of public interest that might otherwise go unreported.   

"If Egypt can put in custody one of its most respected editors and shut down her newsroom, no independent journalist in the country is safe. Attalah must be released immediately, and Mada Masr must be allowed to keep reporting.”  

Licensing dispute  

Attalah was referred for trial on 22 October in Case No. 9072/2026, a day after more than six hours of questioning.   

Prosecutors also questioned her on publishing false news, with questions touching on a Mada Masr report about protests at prisons across the country, but that accusation was dropped from the charge sheet. She had been released on LE100,000 ($1,053) bail.  

Egypt detains entire newsroom of leading fact-checking platform over 'fake news' allegations
Read More »

Founded by Attalah in 2013 and blocked inside Egypt since May 2017, Mada Masr has applied for a licence on multiple occasions since 2018, when a new media law was passed.   

The outlet said it only learned the regulator had rejected its application in 2022, when Attalah was shown the decision while being questioned in another case.   

The Journalists' Syndicate, headed by Khaled al-Balshy, argued that the proper recourse was a challenge before the administrative courts rather than criminal prosecution.    

The case is the sixth brought against Mada Masr, its journalists and editors in six years.   

In August 2025, prosecutors questioned Attalah over "false news" and operating without a licence after the outlet reported alleged abuses at Badr 3 prison.   

In 2022, Attalah and three Mada Masr journalists faced trial for "offending" pro-government lawmakers.  

Security forces raided the outlet's Cairo office in November 2019, briefly detaining Attalah and several colleagues.   

Wider crackdown

The verdict comes less than a month after security forces arrested six journalists from the investigative platform Matsadaash on 28 and 29 September.

Attalah's summons came hours after Mada Masr joined seven other Arab outlets in launching a joint newsroom to fill the gap left by those arrests.

Before the ruling, 119 rights organisations and media institutions condemned what they called an "unprecedented attack on press freedom" in Egypt.

Human Rights Watch said the prosecution raised concerns about licensing requirements being used to restrict independent media. 

Egypt ranks 169th of 180 countries in Reporters Without Borders' 2026 index, which said that despite high-profile releases, including that of writer Alaa Abd el-Fattah, Egypt remains one of the world's biggest jailers of journalists.

item.title: UN inquiry finds Israel committed age-based persecution of Palestinian children in West Bank
item.description:
UN inquiry finds Israel committed age-based persecution of Palestinian children in West Bank

Submitted by Sondos Asem on Tue, 10/27/2026 - 10:25
Investigators say the genocide in Gaza continues while extermination, torture and rape form part of a widespread and systematic attack on Palestinian civilians in the occupied West Bank
Children watch as Israeli security forces deploy nearby in the Palestinian village of al-Mughayyir, near Ramallah in the Israeli-occupied West Bank, on 29 September 2026 (AFP)
Off

Israeli authorities and forces have committed the crime against humanity of age-based persecution against Palestinian children in the occupied West Bank, the UN's top investigative body on Palestine and Israel has concluded, while also accusing Israel of continuing its genocide in Gaza despite a ceasefire agreement.

In its fifth report to the UN General Assembly, published on Monday, the Independent International Commission of Inquiry on the Occupied Palestinian Territory, including East Jerusalem, said Israeli forces had "deliberately killed and caused serious bodily and mental harm to Palestinian children on account of their status as Palestinian children".

The report said the harm inflicted on children "is not incidental or collateral" to the wider violence, but "forms part of a pattern of intentional violence directed against Palestinian children", amounting to the crime against humanity of persecution. 

Between 7 October 2023 and 30 September 2026, Israeli forces killed 1,080 Palestinians in the West Bank, including East Jerusalem, among them at least 237 boys and seven girls, and wounded 10,940, according to UN figures cited in the report.

In one case documented by the commission, a seven-month-old baby was killed and both parents were wounded when an Israeli soldier opened fire on their car in Hebron on 5 June 2026.

Video footage showed the father slowing down, stopping and raising his hands before the soldier fired two rounds into the car without warning, shooting the baby in the head. No medical assistance was provided.

The Israeli army said a member of the Yehuda Brigade had fired because the car accelerated towards soldiers. The commission said that at a range of 10 metres, the soldier would have had a clear view of those inside.

In Tammun, in Tubas Governorate, on 15 March 2026, Israeli forces fired on a car carrying a family of six, killing the mother, father and their two youngest sons. The two older sons were wounded and then assaulted by soldiers.

The commission said it was not aware of any effective investigations, disciplinary or judicial measures in any of the cases it examined, and that the absence of accountability "has entrenched a discriminatory system" in which crimes against Palestinian children are "repeatedly committed with impunity".

The findings come following a damning report by the same commission in June accusing Israeli forces of deliberately targeting Palestinian children as a central element of their genocide in Gaza.

Crimes against humanity

The commission also concluded that Israeli military operations in the West Bank since 7 October 2023, together with settler violence, form a widespread and systematic attack on the civilian population, the constituent element of crimes against humanity.

"The attack requires a high level of coordination and organised planning, indicating the existence of a policy to attack the civilian population," the report said.

"The Commission finds that the Israeli authorities utilised settler violence to target the Palestinian civilian population, and intended settlers’ conduct to form part of the ‘attack’ against the civilian population."

Drones and decomposing babies: What's in UN report on Israel's genocide of Palestinian children
Read More »

The commission added that it considered the killing of Aysenur Eygi, a US and Turkish dual citizen, a crime against humanity as well, because "she was perceived by the Israeli soldiers as part of the targeted population".

It also found that Israeli authorities and forces had committed the crimes against humanity of extermination, other inhumane acts, torture, rape and other forms of sexual violence, and persecution on the grounds of nationality, race and ethnicity.

"The intentional killing and injuring of Palestinian civilians and destruction of homes in the West Bank combined with Israel's persistent denial of responsibility form part of a broader strategy to exterminate and displace Palestinians and impose conditions of life that are unliveable," Srinivasan Muralidhar, the commission's chair, said in a press statement.

The report found that Israeli rules of engagement in the West Bank had been broadened after 7 October 2023 and applied exclusively to Palestinians, while soldiers were prohibited from using lethal force against Jewish Israelis in a similar manner.

It cited Major General Avi Bluth, head of Central Command, as saying in May 2026 that soldiers were "killing like we haven't since 1967".

It also cited Minister of Finance Bezalel Smotrich saying in November 2023 that there are "two million Nazis" in the West Bank, and a year later stating that "the new Nazis have to pay a price in the territory that will be taken from them forever both in Gaza and in Judea and Samaria".

It noted that air strikes have killed 254 Palestinians in the West Bank since 7 October 2023, compared with six between 2008 and that date.

'Soldiers intentionally killed all the victims'

The commission said it investigated seven cases, and documented six others, of killings and acts causing bodily and mental harm against Palestinians between November 2023 and June 2026 as evidence of the more permissive rules of engagement.

"In these cases, the victims were unarmed and did not pose a threat; in the majority of instances, victims were children, including an infant," the report said.

"Israeli personnel used lethal force without warning, targeting victims’ head and/or upper part of their body," it added.

"In all cases, security personnel should have been able to identify that the victim posed no imminent threat. The Commission concludes that Israeli soldiers intentionally killed all the victims."

'In all cases, security personnel should have been able to identify that the victim posed no imminent threat'

- UN inquiry

The commission described Operation Iron Wall, launched in January 2025, as reflecting "the import of the Gaza strategy of total destruction" into the territory.

Military operations since then have caused the largest displacement of Palestinians in the West Bank since 1967, with 34,176 people still displaced as of August 2026.

As an illustrative example of permissive rules of engagement, the commission found that Israel's killing of Turkish-American activist Eygi, shot in the head near Beita on 6 September 2024, amounted to the war crime of wilful killing, concluding that the soldier responsible "deliberately targeted the victim, with the intent to kill her".

It also verified four further cases of sexual violence in Israeli detention since its March 2025 report, including the gang rape of a male detainee with objects at Megiddo prison.

The commission said it applied the same methodology and standard of proof used in its previous investigations, drawing on witness testimony, digital footage, open-source reports and, in some cases, satellite imagery and visual and damage-pattern analysis. 

It sent two requests for information each to Israel and to the State of Palestine. Palestine responded; Israel did not.

Israeli authorities have consistently denied entry visas and access to the commission members, barring them from entering Israel, the West Bank, and Gaza to collect on-the-ground evidence or interview witnesses

Gaza genocide continues

The commission, which already concluded last year that Israel committed genocide in Gaza, found that Israeli authorities and forces "continue to commit genocidal acts with the genocidal intent to destroy, in whole or in part, the Palestinians in Gaza".

Top UN legal investigation concludes Israel is responsible for genocide in Gaza
Read More »

Since the October 2025 ceasefire, Israeli attacks have killed more than 1,431 people, including at least 300 children, and wounded 5,026, figures the report said contradicted claims made to the Security Council that the ceasefire had largely held.

At least 196 Palestinians were killed near the so-called Yellow Line between 10 October 2025 and early April 2026.

The report said the line had become an encroaching de facto border, with Israeli-controlled territory expanding from 53 percent of Gaza to at least 60 percent by September.

"Israel's expansion of territorial control in Gaza continues to result in the killing and harming of Palestinian civilians who approach or cross the Yellow Line," Muralidhar said.

The commission also found that sexual violence, including rape, against two participants in the Global Sumud Flotilla in 2025 amounted to crimes against humanity, including persecution based on gender, sexual orientation and political affiliation.

Examining the root causes of violence, the commission concluded that Israel had "continuously striven to expand territorially and displace Palestinians through violence" since the 1947-48 war, citing Smotrich's September 2025 statement that the principle for applying sovereignty was "maximum land with minimum population".

'Israel's expansion of territorial control in Gaza continues to result in the killing and harming of Palestinian civilians who approach or cross the Yellow Line'

- Srinivasan Muralidhar, commission chair

"Attempting to equate Palestinian statehood with a threat to the existence of Israel is blocking any viable attempts to realize Palestinians' right to self-determination," Muralidhar said.

The commission urged the International Criminal Court (ICC) prosecutor to examine the crimes for possible amendment of existing arrest warrants and future applications. 

In November 2024, the ICC issued arrest warrants for Israel's Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and former Defence Minister Yoav Gallant for war crimes and crimes against humanity committed against Palestinians in Gaza since October 2023. 

More recently, the office of the prosecutor has applied for an arrest warrant for Smotrich over crimes committed against Palestinians in the West Bank, including the crime against humanity of apartheid. 

The ICC has yet to investigate genocide, but the International Court of Justice is currently examining a case brought by South Africa against Israel accusing it of breaching the Genocide Convention in its war on Gaza since 2023. 

Palestinian Authority

The commission found that the State of Palestine had violated the right to life over the killing of a man by Palestinian security forces at a checkpoint in Jenin on 9 December 2024, during the Palestinian Authority's (PA) Operation Protect the Homeland.

It accused the PA of targeting Palestinians who express dissenting views, including journalists and human rights defenders.

It investigated the killing of a female journalism student in the Jenin refugee camp on 28 December 2024, who witnesses said had been threatened by a member of the security forces the previous day.

"Despite an increase in unnecessary or disproportionate use of force since 7 October 2023, the Palestinian Authority has failed to conduct effective and impartial investigations into incidents of killings and to ensure effective remedy, including financial compensation to victims and their family members," Muralidhar said.

item.title: Israeli voter: 'Netanyahu is a psychopath'
item.description:
Israeli voter: 'Netanyahu is a psychopath'

An Israeli voter en route to vote in the city of Or Yehuda, near Tel Aviv, told Middle East Eye that she would be voting for Gadi Eisenkot's Yashar party as "Netanyahu is a psychopath."

Orly Neiger, a 60-year-old physiotherapist and mother-of-two, said she believed Eisenkot and his allies were still right-wing, but nevertheless "people who use their heads - unlike those who vote for Netanyahu out of fear".

She said she would rather have voted for the centre-left The Democrats party led by Yair Golan, but would be casting her vote for Eisenkot as she had "a good friend who works in the Knesset with Eisenkot, and out of respect for his work, I’ll be voting for their list."

"Netanyahu is a psychopath - he’s not a leader," she said.

"He’s incoherent, irresponsible, refuses to take responsibility, fails to see all segments of the nation, and is incapable of engaging with the living, breathing people of Israel."

item.title: Houthis hit Saudi refinery as Iran warns of ‘devastating’ response to further US-Israeli attacks
item.description:
Houthis hit Saudi refinery as Iran warns of ‘devastating’ response to further US-Israeli attacks

Submitted by Elis Gjevori on Tue, 10/27/2026 - 12:02
Saudi-backed forces report strikes on Houthi positions as US embassy warns its citizens to leave the kingdom as attacks intensify
A man cycles past a large billboard displayed in Enghelab Square in Tehran of the Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyhu speaking to an empty UN General Assembly, on 26 October 2026 (Atta Kenare/AFP)
Off

Yemen’s Ansar Allah group, known as the Houthis, said on Tuesday that it had struck Saudi Arabia’s Ras Tanura oil refinery, the kingdom’s largest.

The group’s military spokesperson, Yahya Saree, said a ballistic missile ignited a fire at the Gulf‑side facility, west of the Strait of Hormuz, though Saudi authorities have not confirmed the attack.

The Houthis have intensified strikes on Saudi territory since Riyadh hit Sanaa’s international airport in July, breaking a ceasefire and opening another front in the wider US-Israeli war on Iran.

Saudi Arabia sends almost all its oil exports through two main ports: Ras Tanura on the Gulf and Yanbu on the Red Sea. The Houthis have previously attacked Yanbu.

Bloomberg News reported on Tuesday, citing a source familiar with the matter, that Saudi Arabia had contained a fire near the Ras Tanura oil terminal earlier that day.

Separately, Saudi‑backed Yemeni forces said they had carried out 1,276 operations against Houthi positions in the past 24 hours as part of their “Dawn of Yemen” offensive.

Military spokesperson Colonel Majed al‑Nuzaili said the operations had “neutralised” about 382 Houthi commanders and fighters, without specifying how many were killed or wounded.

He added that the forces had destroyed or damaged 140 military vehicles and heavy weapons, as well as several arms and ammunition depots, and had struck Houthi command centres, defensive positions, reinforcements and supply routes across several fronts.

The US Embassy in Riyadh has told non-emergency government employees and their families to leave Saudi Arabia due to safety risks, an order first issued on 23 October.

In a statement on X, the embassy warned of possible further attacks on airports, airspace closures, flight cancellations and travel disruption. 

'US inability to provide security'

In Iran, Secretary of the Supreme National Security Council Mohsen Rezaei met Supreme Leader Ayatollah Mojtaba Khamenei on Tuesday, state media reported. Khamenei has not appeared in public since succeeding his father, Ali Khamenei, who Israeli-US forces assassinated on 28 February.

Rezaei’s meeting followed talks on Monday with members of the Mecca Alliance - Saudi Defence Minister Prince Khalid bin Salman, Pakistan’s army chief Asim Munir and Turkey’s intelligence chief Ibrahim Kalin - as regional states are seeking to end the war.

Mecca alliance visits Tehran in push to end Israeli-US war and build regional security
Read More »

“Washington’s inability to provide security guarantees has become evident,” Rezaei wrote on X on Tuesday.

“Security in West Asia must originate from within the region itself, and any foreign intervention must be prevented.”

On Monday, at a campaign rally in Corinth, Mississippi, US President Donald Trump defended the war as he faced poor opinion polls ahead of elections that could cost Republicans control of both houses of Congress. He repeated a Republican lawmaker’s false claim that “we didn’t start the war with Iran. Iran started the war with us”.

Trump also defended the war’s economic effects, saying he had expected oil prices to rise much higher.

“I was fully prepared to do it because we really had no choice. Should’ve been done a long time ago,” he said.

Trump said he had never supported ceasefire earlier in the year.

“We did a little ceasefire, which I never liked very much,” he said. “We wanna be nice, but it was just a waste of time as far as I’m concerned.”

He added that Iran had developed missiles capable of reaching Europe and potentially targeting US cities.

'An unstable regional system has been constructed on the entirely false perception that there is a fundamental regional antagonism between Iran and the Arab states of the Gulf'

- Badr al-Busaidi, Omani foreign minister

On Tuesday, Abdollah Haji Sadeghi, Iran supreme leader’s representative to the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps, said Tehran knew “the enemy’s vulnerabilities”. He warned that further US attacks would draw a “harsher and more devastating” response, according to the semi-official Tasnim news agency.

Sadeghi said “the enemy” had wrongly assumed that assassinating Iranian leaders and military commanders would turn public opinion against the government.

After failing militarily, he said, “the enemy” was now using psychological warfare to create “despair, stoking divisions, and casting doubt on resistance”.

Speaking in Cambridge during a diplomatic visit to the UK, Oman's Foreign Minister Badr al-Busaidi called on Gulf states to form a non-aggression pact with Iran, and end the region's reliance on a failed US security umbrella.

"Instead of a genuine security structure designed to maintain stable relations between the eight states of the Gulf, an unstable regional system has been constructed on the entirely false perception that there is a fundamental regional antagonism between Iran and the Arab states of the Gulf," al-Busaidi said.

"There is no such fundamental antagonism. There are problems, yes, of course. But the plain fact is that Arabs and Persians have lived in peace around the Gulf for centuries."
